newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian "power", foreign ministers stay - Interfax.
newsitem.headline: Russian "power", foreign ministers stay - Interfax.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will keep on his defence, security and foreign ministers as well as Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov in a government reshuffle begun on Monday, Interfax news agency said.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said Kulikov would remain as a deputy prime minister in the new cabinet line-up but the fate of the other "power" ministers and of Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov has yet to be officially confirmed.
Interfax quoted sources close to the president saying all the power ministers, including Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, as well as Primakov would stay on.

Nikolai Kovalyov, director of the Federal Security Service (FSB), which succeeded to the internal functions of the KGB keeps his job, the agency said, as does Vyacheslav Trubnikov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
The interior, defence and FSB jobs are collectively known as the "power ministries", in an indication of their strategic importance in a country still prone to political instability.

Further indication that Rodionov and Primakov were safe in the shake-up was given on Monday night when the Kremlin issued a statement saying Yeltsin had passed the international chemical weapons ban treaty to parliament for ratification.
Ministers Rodionov and Primakov would represent the government in the debate, the Kremlin statement said.
Primakov, who spent the weekend in Washington preparing for this week's summit between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton, has looked very secure in his job.
He has won respect at home and abroad for his toughness in asserting Russia's interests combined with subtle diplomacy.
Rodionov came under fire from Yeltsin last month but held an hour-long meeting with him on Monday.
The reshuffle, due to be completed later in the week, was aimed at tackling not just an economic crisis but also the corruption which has left the public disenchanted with reform.
Yeltsin called last month for a revamped cabinet, saying he was dissatisfied with the government's failure to tackle Russia's deep-seated economic and social problems.
But while he acknowledged the government was losing the fight against crime, far from firing Kulikov, he promoted him last month to deputy prime minister and widened his brief.

The new line-up involved sweeping changes bringing in younger, reform-minded people at the top. But the 50-year-old career Interior Ministry soldier, already considered the cabinet's most conservative member, thus stood out even more.
He advocated force against rebels in Chechnya which Yeltsin has admitted was one of the biggest mistakes of his presidency.
But Kulikov, appointed in 1995 and put in charge last month of the tax police, customs service and other agencies dealing with economic crime, is above all loyal to the president.
Kulikov is popular with the police, making him a valuable asset for Yeltsin, especially in view of planned strikes on March 27 which the opposition says could mean widespread unrest.
Yeltsin rapped Rodionov, who took over the defence portfolio last July, for publicly "whining" about the problems facing Russia's demoralised, cash-strapped armed forces.

But they seemed to mend fences on Monday, with Rodionov rowing back on comments last month in which he expressed concern that underfunding of the armed forces raised doubts about the reliabilty of Russia's nuclear weapons.
